title: What does "build for fun" mean to you?
author: Sloptrawler
selftext:
I keep seeing people making their dream game. ARPG, MMO, Puzzle, Souls-like, variants of Pokémon, just whatever. It's an explosion of creativity!

The idea of making an MMO as a solo dev has me thinking...

If you're building the game you always wanted to play, does it matter if anyone else ever plays it?

comments.author: LaidBackDev
comments.body:
If Coding LLMs existed back in 2018 when I first started I would have chosen it over learning coding because the first thing I ever search on Google regarding game dev was "How to make games without coding" but now I just got accustomed to coding that I enjoy the output because I coded it myself even if it's not good. 

Tho I'm not artist so I learning to how to create assets with AI is an upside.

replies.author: steelavian
replies.body: It's funny because I started there. In Klik-n-Play I didn't need to write any code. Eventually I found it so limited I decided to pursue real programming

comments.author: 2ko2ko2
comments.body:
I think there is validity in it, but 99% of people who say they are "making their dream game" are lying (at least to themselves, maybe they actually believe it so it's not an intentional lie).

For example, browse this sub and any other sub about developing with AI and you'll see a post from someone describing how they've been "building their dream game" for a couple of months and have just launched/are preparing to launch their steam page. Some of the posts are actually post launch, and the creator is going over "what went wrong" or wondering why their game isn't getting any traction.

And one look at their "game" and it's blatantly obvious. It's not a game, it's a prototype. The visuals are raw AI outputs with minimal iteration or editing (often with crude and mismatched visual design throughout). If there are animations they are janky. The gameplay systems are either "I combined every mechanic ever into one game" or "I built the most bare bones version of this game like it's still the 80's".

Instead of a game made by a human assisted by AI, they've produced a game made by an AI assisted by a human. 

In my mind I just can't believe this is their "dream game". There's just no way they would stop playing all the games coming out now and that have come out in the last to play this? Cause to me that's what a dream game is. A game that's so perfect to you and your tastes that you could just play it forever (or at least put more hours into it than any other game before. Not dev hours. Pure gameplay).

But once they start complaining about the lack of an audience, or trying to get people to play their game, or looking for strategies to market their game I'm pretty sure I know what's up. What's really going on is that they think they have an idea that can make them money or popular (or both). It's why they rush these projects out the door months, if not years, before they are ready. Why they don't seem to be satisfied with just making their game, other people have to play it too for it to be a success. 

Anyways, TL;DR: No. If you really are building your dream game it shouldn't matter if no one plays it. But I think a lot of people use the phrase to try and avoid criticism when they try to advertise their game. When you are advertising your game to others, it's no longer a passion project only designed for you though. You are trying to sell it to other people, so of course they are going to pick apart everything that they don't like about it, and compare it to other games on the market.

replies.author: Sloptrawler
replies.body:
You raise an interesting point about a person not playing other games because they made their dream game. I think I'm trying to make a card game for myself that I would play for 100 hours, but eventually even my dream game would get old. So, what's the goalpost?  
If I spend 200 hours to make a game that I spend 100 hours enjoying is that good? I think if you enjoy the 200 + 100 it's even better, but then it becomes a solo experience.

I think you're absolutely right though. If you take out the money or recognition, would this still be something a person would make.

comments.author: Aeweisafemalesheep
comments.body:
Unless I see a good game and some damn fine documentation and something about other games that equates to market research plus some video or forum about beta testing, and reiterating, no. People are having something pump out bad prototypes and the hype machines are telling people, that clearly don't game, that bare bones prototypical stuff or an engineer's tech demos are amazing games and that's like me writing up a story board with stick figures, cutting it out, making a flip book and telling you that this is the next blockbuster fucking movie. I sat down and played some demo slop and while some it demos basic mechanic, other stuff is just jankular junk proving that the eggs can be steamed and maybe there's a dash of salt or pepper at best.

The people that are doing something from nothing have some kind of background or have spent the last 120 days not going outside and basically boot camping themselves with all tutor tools possible including the LLM stuff +- hiring help like an artist if they are some coder or vice versa.

I don't doubt that 1 in 1000 will have a decent prototype, especially if the guy is pissed off about something and ends up intstancing up a variant made into a specific direction but most people I am seeing have an idea or lore and have not done any of the fucking design and ludology work nor know how to business nor anything else at all. The not actually hobby guys.

But there will be successfull people in other areas who come to this and do draft the outline, have the bones generated for something, and fill in the stats within their formula craft and have systems that can be applied to say a TTRPG or whatever and that kinda guy has been doing kinds of work for a while to have the taste use essentially what's a very dynamic template if we're being kind and we know the other arguments.

But i'm sorry, saying hey LLM, do asteroids or whatever but green and the astroids are pop corn is not a dream game. That's the flappy bird era of clones.

There's also shit like playing games and doing market research and understanding a genre, audience and all this other stuff man. If i want a community game. I'd better know a thing.
